overview: Nine Department of State “List of Papers” index sheets summarize correspondence filed from 1940 through 1943 concerning Japanese merchant shipping. The entries trace commercial services and shipbuilding intelligence, Japanese government requisition and diversion of vessels, cargo claims involving American and Dutch interests, Panama Canal movements, and requests for immunity from legal process for government-controlled ships. Recurring cases concern the TATUTA/TATSUTA MARU and SANYO MARU, while later entries reflect wartime losses, shipping shortages, and intelligence gathering.

subfiles.title: List of papers: shipping restrictions and consular reports, entries 550–552
subfiles.about: Indexes early 1940 reports on Shandong coastal restrictions and Japanese shipping at Canton, Whampoa, and Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records the reported abolition of shipping restrictions along part of the Shandong Peninsula and the Department’s acknowledgment of the Japanese Embassy’s notification. It also indexes reports on Japanese military transports and commercial movements at Canton and Whampoa, as well as new difficulties in shipping reporting at Kobe.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Japanese services, shipbuilding, and tonnage acquisition, entries 553–562
subfiles.about: Indexes reports on Japanese shipbuilding data, overseas steamship services, and efforts to acquire additional tonnage.
subfiles.summary: The entries cover reporting difficulties and the nonavailability of commercial ship-construction figures in Japan. Other papers concern Japanese services to Latin America and Central America, the Panama Canal routing of ships, and financing arranged through the China Foreign Trade Corporation to acquire vessels for Japan. The sheet also notes a new service between French Indochina and Japan, inaugurated at Haiphong.

subfiles.title: List of papers: cargo appeals for Tatsuta Maru and Haiki Maru
subfiles.about: Indexes commercial requests to unload American-owned cargo from Japanese vessels on the Pacific Coast.
subfiles.summary: Most entries are telegrams from commercial firms seeking assistance in unloading cargo carried by the TATUTA MARU or HAIKI MARU at San Francisco. The sheet also lists reports denying rumors about oil loading at Houston and requesting the discharge of American-owned cargo from Japanese ships on the Pacific Coast.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Panama Canal delays and requisitioned Japanese ships
subfiles.about: Indexes reports on Japanese shipping to South America, Canal passage delays, and requisitioned vessels.
subfiles.summary: The sheet includes a report on continued Japanese steamship service to South America and additional cargo-unloading requests. It records that three Japanese steamers were held on the Atlantic side of the Panama Canal while six others were approaching, together with information given to the Japanese Ambassador. Further entries concern the KONGO MARU and AYUMASAN MARU and a War Department weekly report on Japanese shipping.

subfiles.title: List of papers: requisitions, diversions, and detentions, entries 641–647
subfiles.about: Indexes policy correspondence on Japanese ship requisitions, cargo diversions, and the detention or treatment of vessels and passengers.
subfiles.summary: The entries include State Department encouragement of monthly reports on Japanese shipping and a note about an American missionary detained aboard the TATUTA MARU. Sumner Welles reported a conversation with the Japanese Ambassador about Japanese steamers detained at Cristóbal. The sheet also covers ships and American cargoes diverted by Japanese government orders, an inquiry to the embassy in Tokyo, and the treatment of Japanese vessels in Australian waters.

subfiles.title: List of papers: immunity and port entry for government-controlled ships
subfiles.about: Indexes legal correspondence concerning immunity, requisition dates, and the TATSUTA MARU’s entry into Balboa.
subfiles.summary: Robert L. Werner asked what immunity the TATUTA MARU might enjoy from legal process because of its mission. Other correspondence sought information on the requisition dates of the BORDEAUX MARU, NAKO MARU, AZUMASAN MARU, KONGO MARU, KINIKAWA MARU, KOGYU MARU, and NANKAI MARU. Japan requested immunity from federal, state, and territorial jurisdiction for the TATUTA, HIKAWA, and TAIYO, while the War Department raised no objection to the TATSUTA MARU entering Balboa.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Sanyo Maru cargo and wartime shipping intelligence, entries 675–688
subfiles.about: Indexes investigations of SANYO MARU cargo alongside reports on Japanese shipbuilding, requisitioned ships, and wartime fleet conditions.
subfiles.summary: Several entries concern cargo discharged from the SANYO MARU at New York in May 1940 and subsequent requests by Dutch representatives and U.S. agencies for information. The sheet also lists documents about the requisitioned TATUTA MARU, shipping conditions at Nagasaki after December 1941, and British information on Japanese merchant-ship construction. Joseph P. Tumulty Jr. sought lists of vessel-owning companies and historical data on Japanese shipping before the war.

subfiles.title: List of papers: Dutch claims to Sanyo Maru cargo, entries 689–695
subfiles.about: Indexes Treasury and Netherlands Embassy correspondence about SANYO MARU cargo and Chinese intelligence on Japanese merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department and Netherlands Embassy exchanged repeated communications about cargo landed from the SANYO MARU in New York, including whether information could be released. Chinese communications supplied information on the construction and operation of Japanese merchant vessels. Later entries seek the quantities, disposition, and sale proceeds of specified cargo lots in which the Netherlands Shipping and Trading Committee had an interest.

subfiles.title: List of papers: cargo disposition, Tatsuta Maru sinking, and shipping shortage, entries 697–704
subfiles.about: Indexes final SANYO MARU cargo inquiries, a Japanese shipping-company bankruptcy, and wartime reports on the TATUTA MARU and Japan’s shipping shortage.
subfiles.summary: The first entries continue the Treasury and Netherlands Embassy investigation of merchandise discharged from the SANYO MARU, including reports from the New York customs collector. The sheet also records a request concerning the bankruptcy of a Japanese shipping company. Later entries report the TATUTA MARU’s sinking off Chefoo on October 1 and transmit Gunther Stein’s article “Japan’s Shipping Shortage” from The Manchester Guardian.

interest: These sheets provide a compact roadmap to a much larger body of correspondence and are especially useful where the underlying papers are missing, dispersed, or cross-filed. They show the rapid shift from routine monitoring of commercial routes and ship construction in 1940 to cargo seizures, government requisition, immunity disputes, and wartime intelligence by 1941–43. The extended SANYO MARU sequence illuminates the slow interagency handling of neutral Dutch commercial claims, while the TATUTA/TATSUTA MARU entries connect passenger detention, sovereign-immunity claims, special port access, requisition, and eventual wartime loss.
